first.rationale: The two metrics actually degrading are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and memory_86 plus memory_31 both point at the onboarding/signup path as the highest-leverage lever for exactly those metrics. That makes simplify_onboarding the direction that attacks the observed regression at its source rather than papering over it. I am verifying memory_86 and memory_31 because both are consolidated summaries whose stated wins are measured in funnel-stage metrics (completion, time-to-value, first-week activation) rather than in qualified revenue, which is the actual objective; I need the original records to see whether downstream revenue or lead quality was ever measured or whether it was silently unchanged/negative. Specifically, memory_31's 'cutting required fields at signup' is the classic case where an activation lift is bought with worse lead qualification and routing, so more accounts activate while fewer become qualified revenue — that is the downstream value risk I am flagging and will instrument for. I am spending the third pull on memory_73 rather than acting on it, because promotional_pricing is the reflexive answer to the competitor's entry pricing and its summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') is the one most likely to have shed caveats about margin, discount-cohort retention, and permanent price-anchor damage; if the source record shows those were never tracked, that direction stays off the table this week regardless of competitive pressure. Answering a price attack with price is also the move most likely to trade sustainable revenue for a quarter of volume. Referral incentive (memory_57) and enterprise sales assist (memory_44) are plausible but neither addresses the two declining metrics, so they lose the single slot on relevance. I am running this at standard_experiment scale with a holdout, and reading out on downstream qualified-revenue and lead-quality metrics rather than completion rate alone — a small guarded test would not resolve the quality question, and a broad rollout would commit the funnel to an unverified inherited claim. If verification shows memory_31's lift came with unmeasured or degraded lead quality, I will narrow to memory_86's step-reduction variant and leave qualifying fields intact.

final.rationale:
Verification substantially changed the picture on one direction and confirmed another. exp_73 is the decisive finding: the inherited summary said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and silently dropped the source record's explicit warning — 30-day retention -12% and a cohort that does not survive the first renewal cycle, with a stated instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Since my objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is ruled out even though it is the most direct-looking answer to the competitor's entry pricing. Meeting a price attack with a discount would buy signups that churn before renewal and would additionally anchor the segment's price expectations downward. The consolidated memory was actively misleading here, which is worth recording back.

exp_86 came back clean and is the strongest available option: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — a rare case where the funnel-stage win is corroborated by a downstream durability signal rather than contradicted by one. It also targets both metrics that are actually regressing (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), so it treats the observed decline at its source. I am therefore running shortened onboarding, structured as exp_86's step/flow reduction.

exp_31 is real but narrower and dirtier: it holds only on SMB, explicitly did not replicate on other segments, and carried retention -1% against qualified revenue +4%. That is the pattern I flagged in advance — cutting required signup fields trades some lead qualification for volume. So I am deliberately not bundling field-cutting into this test. I keep qualifying fields intact and reduce onboarding steps only, which preserves the exp_86 result's clean retention profile instead of contaminating it with exp_31's known downside. If the onboarding test reads out well, SMB-scoped field reduction is a defensible follow-up, but it should not ride along untracked inside this slot.

Standard experiment scale with a holdout. A small guarded test cannot resolve whether the lift persists to qualified revenue, and a broad rollout would over-commit on two data points from earlier conditions. Primary readout is qualified revenue and 30-day retention, not completion rate alone; completion is the mechanism, not the objective, and exp_73 is the standing proof that a headline funnel metric can move hard in the right direction while the underlying value moves the wrong way. Residual uncertainty: both source experiments predate the current competitive environment, so a confirmed prior lift may attenuate now that price-sensitive SMB accounts are being pulled away for reasons onboarding cannot fix. Onboarding does not answer the competitor's pricing directly, and I am accepting that gap rather than closing it with a discount that verification shows destroys the cohort.
